description: Mercury is a Digital Radio OFDM protocol for HF broadcast and peer-to-peer ARQ connections with compatible TCP interfaces

latest_release.name: Mercury 1.9.25
latest_release.body:
> [!WARNING]
> **1.9.25 does not connect to 1.9.24 or any older version, in either direction.** Upgrade every station you talk to at once, and the gateways first. Which versions talk to each other: [Discussion #637](https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/discussions/637).

**Mercury transmits 4 dB louder.** On an sBitx that is about 2.5 times the power at the same setting; `[audio] tx_gain_db = -4` keeps the 1.9.24 level. Each bandwidth has a ladder of its own on faster modes, plus fixes for BPQ32, Pat and Winlink Express.

What changed, what was tested and what to check before upgrading: **[docs/RELEASE-1.9.25.md](https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/blob/v1.9.25/docs/RELEASE-1.9.25.md)**

## What's Changed
* host: the daemon build defines #534's two audioio calls; CI links it by @rafael2k in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/549
* ci: run the unit tests on macOS arm64 by @thagale in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/551
* Add libxxf86vm-dev for fyne-ui to Linux build instructions by @tarantir in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/557
* docs: Winlink gateways with Mercury by @pedromessetti in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/563
* fix: don't read rig_caps.macro_name from a mismatched Hamlib (#568) by @pedromessetti in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/573
* radio_io: reopen a network rig's Hamlib session after its server restarts by @armysarge in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/571
* arq: after an ABORT, hold a scanning host until our one DISCONNECT is out by @pedromessetti in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/560
* arq: a CALL whose listening gap has gone is not answered by @pedromessetti in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/559
* audioio: with pulse, "default" lets PulseAudio choose the device by @pedromessetti in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/576
* radio_io: reopen a network rig's Hamlib session on a timeout too by @pedromessetti in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/574
* arq: the DISCONNECT deferral log shows the cap in force by @pedromessetti in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/582
* tcp: drop idle data-port bytes when their data client leaves (#572) by @pedromessetti in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/580
* tnc: a web browser on the control port is told so and closed by @pedromessetti in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/583
* Comment on reset clients in the broadcast backlog by @armysarge in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/588
* arq: a DISCONNECT that is never retried goes twice to a marginal peer by @pedromessetti in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/586
* windows-installer: an upgrade keeps the station's mercury.ini by @pedromessetti in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/594
* tcp: a host write is held, not dropped, in a call; the reactor never waits on the session lock by @rafael2k in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/590
* modem: clip QAM16C2 like the other data modes (on air: 58 of 64 frames against none) by @rafael2k in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/575
* carousel: size the poll that rides with an ack and a round for the answer by @rafael2k in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/596
* arq: ABORT cuts the keydown on the air short by @pedromessetti in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/592
* modem, carousel: a ladder per bandwidth on a faster geometry; thresholds on the accurate S/N scale by @rafael2k in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/599
* arq: BUFFER counts a floor block as in at its BREAK, never 0 early by @pedromessetti in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/593
* tnc: opt-in absorb of Winlink Express's P2P idle DISCONNECT (#392) by @pedromessetti in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/581
* modem, carousel: a 2 kHz MFSK as rung 1 of BW2300 and BW2750 by @rafael2k in https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/pull/602
* tests: #579 regression -- the reactor never waits on the s

detail.readme:
# Mercury — HERMES HF Modem Mercury is part of the [HERMES project](https://hermes.radio/) (High-Frequency Emergency and Rural Multimedia Exchange System) by [Rhizomatica](https://www.rhizomatica.org/), funded by [ARDC](https://www.ardc.net/) and others. Mercury is a software modem for sending email, files and messages over HF radio — the kind of link you have when there is no internet, no phone network and no power grid worth speaking of. **Start here:** [Getting Started](#getting-started-with-mercury) · [Graphical interfaces](#graphical-interfaces) · [Configuration](#configuration-file) · [Docs](https://rhizomatica.github.io/mercury/) · [Mailing list](https://lists.riseup.net/www/info/hermes-general) · [Google Play (Android)](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=org.rhizomatica.mercury) · [App Store (iPhone, iPad)](https://apps.apple.com/app/mercury-hf-modem/id6822504870) **Help wanted: Apple hardware.** We build and test the macOS and iOS apps in a macOS virtual machine on an Intel PC, so we have never run the arm64 builds on real Apple hardware with a radio ourselves. Any ARM64 Apple device helps: an Apple Silicon Mac (M1 or later), an iPhone or an iPad, and any donation is welcome. Please write to the [mailing list](https://lists.riseup.net/www/info/hermes-general) or open an [issue](https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury/issues). ## What this software does Mercury turns a single-sideband radio into a data link. It handles the waveform, the error correction, the retransmissions and the radio keying, and presents the result to your application as an ordinary TCP connection. - **ARQ data link for point-to-point sessions** — a connect/accept handshake, an erasure-coded "carousel" that the receiver drives (Reed-Solomon blocks, so a lost frame is replaced by any other frame of the block rather than resent), and a controlled disconnect, so a file either arrives intact or you are told it did not. - **Adaptive speed** — each direction runs on one of seven rungs of its bandwidth's ladder; at BW2300, from the 32-tone MFSK floor through MFSK2K, DATAC4, DATAC3, DATAC1 and DATAC17 up to QAM16C2 (BW500 and BW2750 ladders: [docs/MODES.md](docs/MODES.md)). It starts on the rung the connect's SNR supports and moves on measured delivery. Control frames ride DATAC16 (and MFSK, or tone patterns, at the floor), so signalling survives when payload cannot. - **Broadcast mode** alongside ARQ, with its own framing and TCP ingress port — used for one-to-many traffic and for [Reticulum](#reticulum) mesh networking. - **VARA-style TCP TNC interface** on two sockets (control on the base port, data on base+1), speaking `MYCALL`, `LISTEN`, `CONNECT`, `BUFFER`, `SN`, `BITRATE`, `TUNE` (a 1 kHz ATU tuning carrier with a hard 60 s unkey timer) and `MONITOR` (a passive VARA-style monitor that decodes every mode). Existing VARA-aware software can generally talk to Mercury unchanged. - **Runs on the audio hardware you have** — `alsa`, `pulse`, `oss`, `coreaudio`, `aaudio`, `dsound`, `wasapi`, `rtp` (to hermes-radio-daemon), `hl2` (a [Hermes-Lite 2](docs/HERMES-LITE-2.md) on the network, with no sound card or CAT), plus `shm`, `null`, `fifo` and `sock` for embedded and test use. - **Keys the radio for you** via Hamlib, serial RTS (including DigiRig), or the HERMES shared-memory interface — or stays out of the way and lets your client do it. Mercury runs on Linux, Windows and macOS, including Raspberry Pi. **On-air compatibility.** 1.9.20 and later (the "2.0" architecture) connect to each other, but not to 1.9.19 or older in either direction: their connect frames have a packet type of their own (and 1.9.18 and 1.9.19 did not connect to each other either). A station with `mfsk_tx_only` set needs 1.9.21 or later at the other end. See [docs/RELEASE-1.9.24.md](docs/RELEASE-1.9.24.md), [docs/RELEASE-1.9.23.md](docs/RELEASE-1.9.23.md), [docs/RELEASE-1.9.22.md](docs/RELEASE-1.9.22.md), [docs/RELEASE-1.9.21.md](docs/RELEASE-1.9.21.md), [docs/RELEASE-1.9.20.md](docs/RELEASE-1.9.20.md), [docs/RELEASE-1.9.19.md](docs/RELEASE-1.9.19.md) and [docs/UPGRADING-TO-1.9.18.md](docs/UPGRADING-TO-1.9.18.md) before upgrading. ## Command-line reference Most settings live in `mercury.ini` (see [Configuration File](#configuration-file)); command-line flags override it. Run `./mercury -h` for this list at any time.
All command-line options (click to expand) ``` Usage modes: ./mercury -m [mode_index] -i [device] -o [device] -x [sound_system] -p [arq_tcp_base_port] -b [broadcast_tcp_port] -f [freedv_verbosity] -H [hamlib_log_level] -k [rx_input_channel] [-P ptt_method] [-A ptt_device] [-G] [-T] [-U ui_port] [-W] [-d] ./mercury [-h -l -z -K -Q -V] Options: -c [cpu_nr] Run on CPU [cpu_nr]. Use -1 to disable CPU selection, which is the default. -m [mode_index] Startup payload mode index shown in "-l" output. Used for broadcast and idle/disconnected ARQ decode. Default is 1 (DATAC3) -s [mode_index] Legacy alias for -m. -f [freedv_verbosity] FreeDV modem verbosity level (0..3). Default is 0. -H [hamlib_log_level] Hamlib radio log level (0..6). Default is 0. -k [rx_input_channel] Capture input channel: left, right, or stereo. Default is left. -i [device] Radio Capture device id (eg: "plughw:0,0"). -o [device] Radio Playback device id (eg: "plughw:0,0"). -x [sound_system] Sets the sound system or IO API to use: alsa, pulse, oss, coreaudio, aaudio, dsound, wasapi, hl2, shm, rtp, null, fifo or sock. Default is alsa on Linux, dsound on Windows. null, fifo and sock are developer/test backends; fifo uses raw s32le PCM at 8 kHz via -i/-o paths; sock is a framed, virtual-clock lockstep transport (MERCURY_AUDIO_SOCK=). rtp exchanges the radio signal with hermes-radio-daemon as RTP multicast: -i [,iface] (default 239.255.72.1,lo), -o (default 239.255.72.2); PTT travels in the TX stream. hl2 uses a Hermes-Lite 2 on the network as radio and sound card: -i auto (the first that answers a broadcast) or -i [:port]; set its frequency with -F (or [hl2] in the INI). -F [frequency_hz] Hermes-Lite 2 (-x hl2) dial frequency in Hz, upper sideband. Without one it receives but never transmits. -p [arq_tcp_base_port] Sets the ARQ TCP base port (control is base_port, data is base_port + 1). Default is 8300. -b [broadcast_tcp_port] Sets the broadcast TCP port. Default is 8100. -U [ui_port] Sets the UI port (WebSocket port). Default is 10000. Requires -G. -W Disable waterfall/spectrum data sent to the UI (used to spare CPU). Requires -G. -G Enable UI communication (WebSocket server for mercury-qt). Off by default. -T Use WSS (WebSocket Secure/TLS) for UI communication. Requires -G. Default uses plain WS (no TLS). -l Lists all modulator/coding modes. -z Lists all available sound cards. -v Verbose mode. Prints more information during execution. -d Trace mode. Logs the raw bytes of every decoded connect frame (implies -v). -L Write log to file (TIMING level and above). Windows default: logs\mercury_engine.log beside mercury.exe. -J Use JSONL format for log file (requires -L). -P [ptt_method] PTT method: none, hamlib, serial, cm108, or hermes_shm. -R [radio_model] Sets HAMLIB radio model and selects Hamlib PTT. -A [ptt_device] PTT serial device or HAMLIB device/ip:port endpoint. -S Select HERMES shared-memory PTT (Linux shorthand for -P hermes_shm). -C [config_file] Path to init configuration file (INI format). Default is mercury.ini in the current directory, else $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/mercury/mercury.ini (~/.config/mercury/mercury.ini), else /etc/mercury/mercury.ini. A file that is there but cannot be read in full stops the modem. -K List HAMLIB supported radio models. -Q Test PTT: key the configured backend for one second, release it, and exit. -t Test TX mode. -r Test RX mode. -V Print version information and exit. -h Prints this help. ```
Mode behavior notes: - `-m` / `-s` sets the mode for **broadcast**, for the **test** modes, and for what the payload decoder listens on while no ARQ session is up. It does not affect an ARQ session. `mercury -l` lists the indices: 0 DATAC1, 1 DATAC3, 2 DATAC0, 3 DATAC4, 4 DATAC13, 5 DATAC14, 6 FSK_LDPC, 7 DATAC15, 8 DATAC16, 9 DATAC17, 10 QAM16C2, 11 MFSK, 12 MFSK500, 13 DATAC17W, 14 QAM16C2W, 15 DATAN1, 16 QAM16N1, 17 QAM16N2, 18 MFSK2K. - During an ARQ session, control frames normally use DATAC16, and each direction's payload runs on the rungs of the session's bandwidth: at BW2300 MFSK (MFSK500 on the deep floor), MFSK2K, DATAC4, DATAC3, DATAC1, DATAC17, QAM16C2; the BW500 and BW2750 ladders are in [docs/MODES.md](docs/MODES.md). The start rung comes from the SNR measured on the connect; see [docs/CAROUSEL-ARQ.md](docs/CAROUSEL-ARQ.md). - VARA `BW500` keeps the link narrow. The negotiated bandwidth selects one of the three seven-rung payload ladders. - `CALL` advertises the local BW token and `ACCEPT` returns the negotiated session token. If either side uses `BW500`, the link stays narrow; `BW2750` is preserved in `CONNECTED ... BW` only when both peers advertise it. - `FSK_LDPC` is currently **experimental** (mainly for lab/test usage), may have longer decode/sync latency depending on setup, and is not recommended for production links yet. - `[arq] mfsk_tx_only = true` makes the station transmit MFSK only (CALL/ACCEPT, control and payload) for radios that can only key FSK — the QRP Labs QDX, QRPguys AFSK III and similar. Its peers keep its transmit direction on the MFSK floor rung for the whole session; receive is unaffected, so the cost is throughput, not reach. Such a station connects only to releases after 1.9.20; the others still connect to 1.9.20. - `[arq] max_keydown_s = 16` holds every transmission of the station to 16 s, a poll sent before a round included, for TCP clients that abort when PTT stays on too long. **vARIM 1.13 and later need no setting:** they allow 35 s keyed, longer than any Mercury transmission (30 s at most). vARIM before 1.13 gives up after about 20 s keyed, and a full DATAC3 round is 25-30 s (#445). With such a vARIM, set it on every station that runs it: it holds the station's own transmissions and asks the peer for short rounds, but a peer without it can still key longer (a poll before a round, its own floor rounds). The peer needs no update to talk to it. The cost is throughput: in the simulator, about 0-6 % on fast channels and 13-30 % on slow ones and at BW500 (8 KB both ways). `0`, the default, keeps the protocol's 30 s; the MFSK floor's single frame (13.5 s, 27 s on the BW500 floor) is never split, so a BW500 session that falls to its floor still keys for 27 s. PTT control notes: - The default method is `none`; Mercury then leaves radio keying to the TCP client. - `-P serial -A COM7` (or a POSIX device such as `/dev/ttyUSB0`) keys a serial modem-control line. No baud rate is used. Which line, and whether it is inverted, comes from `[ptt] line` and `[ptt] invert` — RTS non-inverted by default. - `-P cm108` keys a GPIO pin on a CM108/CM119-class USB sound chip. The device is auto-detected; `[ptt] cm108_gpio` selects the pin (default 3). - `-R` is the compatible Hamlib shorthand: it selects the model and the `hamlib` PTT method. `-A` supplies its device or `ip:port`, and `-K` lists models. - `-S` is the compatible shorthand for `hermes_shm` and is unavailable on Windows builds. - `-Q` opens the configured backend, keys it for one second, releases it, and exits without starting the modem or audio devices. For example: `mercury -C mercury.ini -Q`. Sound card notes: - A capture device that stops delivering audio is reopened every 2 s. After three reopens in a row that bring nothing (about 6 s, not counting the time Mercury is transmitting), Mercury logs `the capture device delivers no audio` once and reports the audio as failed (`audio_ok: false` in the GUI and the WebSocket status) until samples come back. When they do, the log says how long the station was deaf: `capture delivering again after reopen #N (S s without audio)`. - When it reports the failure, and on every 5th reopen after that, Mercury also lists the sound cards again and looks for the device by the name it had when capture started. Windows can give a USB codec a new id, under the same name, when it resets or is re-plugged. If exactly one device has that name, Mercury opens it under its new id (`listed under a new id: ... -- opening that`). If two have it (two radios with the same codec), Mercury does not guess, and asks you to select it again. The default device (no `-i`) is left to the sound system. - The same at start, on Windows (`wasapi`, `dsound`): when you choose the devices in the GUI, their names are saved next to their ids (`input_device_name`, `output_device_name` in `mercury.ini`). If a saved id is no longer listed when Mercury starts, the device with that exact name is used, if exactly one has it (`device id '...' is gone; found '...' by its saved name`). `-i` and `-o` on the command line drop the saved name. A config without the names works as before. - A playback device that takes no audio for 1 s while Mercury has audio to send is reopened, and what was queued meanwhile is dropped, so later transmissions stay inside their PTT. After three reopens in a row that bring nothing, the GUI shows `playback: the playback device takes no audio (still trying it)`. - PulseAudio (`-x pulse`): if a transmission after a long idle spell keys the radio but sends no audio (seen with a USB card on PipeWire, issue #591), set `[audio] pulse_keepalive = true`. Mercury then feeds the playback stream with silence between transmissions, as VARA and WSJT-X do. It is off by default: it costs a little CPU while idle and keeps the card from suspending. Transmit level and power notes: - Since 1.9.25 every mode peaks at about −2 dBFS: the OFDM modes at −2.0 dBFS and MFSK at −2.5 dBFS, measured at the sound card with `tx_gain_db` at 0 (1.9.24 peaked at −6 dBFS). `[audio] tx_gain_db` trims around that level, and `-4` gives back the 1.9.24 drive. `TUNE ` keys a steady 1 kHz tone at an absolute level that `tx_gain_db` doesn't touch. `TUNE -2` therefore shows the RF power your frames peak at. - **sBitx (hermes-radio-daemon):** the power setting is the share of the PA's output for a full-scale signal, so Mercury's frames now get most of what the setting allows. An ARQ session keys often (about 25 transmissions in 10 minutes), so a PA run near saturation gets hot. Start low (20-40 %), and read the real output while keyed with `sbitx_client -c get_fwd` (watts × 10) and `get_ref` (SWR × 10), or during a `TUNE -2`. Raise the setting only while the radio stays cool. One field sBitx V3 saturated at about 10-14 W and ran hot at 85 % in a long A/B. - **Radios with ALC on a USB sound card** (IC-7100 and most transceivers): set the radio's power, and let the ALC level the audio. OFDM frames, whose peaks sit 7-8 dB above their mean, kept an IC-7100's ALC around 0.88 of its range. The short MFSK frames (CALLs, acknowledgements) reached the top of it: a constant-envelope signal carries more average power for the same peak. If the ALC is pinned on those, lower the drive with `tx_gain_db -2`, or with the radio's USB modulation level. - **Radios without ALC on a sound card** (uBitx and similar): more drive past the PA's linear range gives a weaker, wider signal, not a stronger one. Find the knee with a `TUNE` sweep at increasing dBFS, measured at the other station or on an SDR. One uBitx gave its strongest tone at `TUNE -20` (with its sound card's Master at −5 dB) and dropped, splattering, above it. Then set the sound card's playback level, or `tx_gain_db`, so that Mercury's −2 dBFS peaks land at the knee. ## Getting Started with Mercury ### Compile and Install from Git repository on Linux 1. Install the dependencies: ```bash sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install build-essential pkg-config libasound2-dev libpulse-dev libhamlib-dev make git ``` 2. Clone Mercury GitHub repository: ```bash git clone https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury.git ``` 3. Change directory to `mercury/`: ```bash cd mercury ``` 4. Build mercury (edit `config.mk` first if you need a custom compiler or flags; defaults are fine for most): ```bash make ``` 5. Install system-wide: ```bash sudo make install ``` The FreeDV codec is vendored in-tree — no external FreeDV or codec2 packages are needed. ### Build targets | Target | Description | |--------|-------------| | `make` / `make all` | Build the standalone CLI `mercury` binary | | `make libmercury_core.a` | Compile all Mercury C objects into a host-arch static library (used by `fyne-ui`) | | `make fyne-ui` | Build the single-binary native GUI (`mercury-ui`), embedding the engine via CGo. Requires `make libmercury_core.a` first. **Needs Go** ([setup](#gui-build-prerequisites-go--fyne)). | | `make libmercury_core_w64.a` | Cross-compile Mercury C objects for Windows x64 (requires `gcc-mingw-w64-x86-64`) | | `make fyne-ui-windows` | Cross-compile the single-binary GUI to `mercury-ui.exe`. Depends on `libmercury_core_w64.a`. **Needs Go** ([setup](#gui-build-prerequisites-go--fyne)). | | `make windows-installer` | Full Windows installer pipeline: cross-compile engine + GUI, copy DLLs, patch config. Output goes to `windows-installer/`. Requires MinGW + Go. | | `make windows-zip` | Build standalone CLI + GUI Windows binaries and zip them for distribution | | `make fyne-ui-macos` | Package `Mercury.app` for the host architecture (run on macOS). **Needs Go + the `fyne` CLI** ([setup](#gui-build-prerequisites-go--fyne)). | | `make fyne-ui-macos-dmg` | Wrap the host-arch `Mercury.app` in a drag-to-install `Mercury.dmg` at the repo top level. **Needs Go + the `fyne` CLI** ([setup](#gui-build-prerequisites-go--fyne)). | | `make fyne-ui-macos-universal-dmg` | **Distribution build:** universal (x86_64 + arm64) `Mercury.app` wrapped in `Mercury.dmg` at the repo top level. This is the artifact for the website. **Needs Go + the `fyne` CLI** ([setup](#gui-build-prerequisites-go--fyne)). | | `make fyne-ui-macos-appstore-pkg` | **Mac App Store build:** the universal `Mercury.app` for macOS 15.0+, sandboxed (`macos/entitlements-appstore.plist`), signed with `MACOS_APPSTORE_IDENTITY` and the profile in `MACOS_APPSTORE_PROFILE`, in an installer package signed with `MACOS_INSTALLER_IDENTITY`, for upload to App Store Connect. | | `make test` | Build and run the C unit and simulator tests (`tests/`). | | `make integration-test` | Run the Go two-daemon integration tests ([tests/integration](tests/integration/README.md)); `make integration-test-random` uses a fresh channel seed. | ### Build options Passed on the `make` command line, e.g. `make HAVE_HAMLIB=0`. | Option | Effect | |--------|--------| | `HAVE_HAMLIB=0` | Build without Hamlib. Drops the `libhamlib-dev` build dependency entirely; `-P hamlib`, `-R` and `-K` are compiled out and report "HAMLIB support not compiled in". The serial/RTS, CM108 and HERMES shared-memory PTT backends are unaffected, so the radio can still be keyed. | | `HAVE_HIDAPI=0` | Build without hidapi. The CM108 GPIO PTT backend then talks to `/dev/hidraw` directly, which works on Linux only. | Both are auto-detected with `pkg-config` when not set, so the default build picks them up if they are installed. Set them to `0` to opt out. **If the build fails on `hamlib/rig.h: No such file or directory`** while `libhamlib-dev` is installed, the package's headers are missing or broken — Mercury only enables Hamlib when `pkg-config --exists hamlib` succeeds, so pkg-config is finding the `.pc` file but the headers it points at are not there. Either reinstall the package (`sudo apt reinstall libhamlib-dev`) or build without it using `HAVE_HAMLIB=0`. ### Build the Fyne GUI (Linux) ```bash sudo apt install golang-go pkg-config libhamlib-dev libpulse-dev libasound2-dev libssl-dev libhidapi-dev \ libgl1-mesa-dev libegl1-mesa-dev xorg-dev libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev make fyne-ui ./mercury-ui ``` ### Build the Android .apk or .aab (technology preview) ```sh # Android NDK r27d, the Android SDK (platform 34, build-tools 34) and Go. # The Makefile builds its own copy of the fyne CLI, at Android 8 (API 26) # as the minimum (.fyne-android/). Source RPMs are in `http://debian.hermes.radio/sailfish/source/`. ## Configuration File Mercury reads an INI-format configuration file at startup. Command-line arguments take priority over values from the file. With `-C ` that file is used. Otherwise Mercury takes the first of these that exists (on Windows, only the first): 1. `mercury.ini` in the current working directory 2. `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/mercury/mercury.ini`, or `~/.config/mercury/mercury.ini` when `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is not set 3. `/etc/mercury/mercury.ini` A configuration that cannot be read in full (it does not parse, or a setting has an invalid value) stops Mercury with the reason before the modem starts: running on part of a configuration could open the wrong sound device or key the wrong radio. `-h`, `-V`, `-l`, `-z` and `-K` still work. With no configuration file (none found, or the `-C` file does not exist), Mercury runs on its built-in defaults and the command line, and says so, naming the sound system and devices it opens. See the included [mercury.ini.example](mercury.ini.example) for all available settings and their default values (the Debian package installs it as `/usr/share/doc/mercury/mercury.ini.example`). Copy it to one of the places above and edit it for your radio, for example: ```sh mkdir -p ~/.config/mercury cp /usr/share/doc/mercury/mercury.ini.example ~/.config/mercury/mercury.ini ``` PTT is configured independently of CAT-oriented radio settings: ```ini [ptt] method = serial device = COM7 ``` Valid methods are `none`, `hamlib`, `serial`, `cm108`, and `hermes_shm` (`serial_rts` is still accepted and means `serial` with `line = rts`). Legacy `radio_model`, `radio_device`, `radio_serial_speed`, and `hamlib_log_level` keys are still read and mapped to the equivalent PTT configuration. #### Common interfaces | Interface | Method | Settings | |---|---|---| | DigiRig Mobile | `serial` | `line = rts` (default) | | All-In-One Cable (AIOC) | `serial` | `line = both`, `invert = rts` | | All-In-One Cable (AIOC) | `cm108` | auto-detected, `cm108_gpio = 3` | | CM108/CM119 USB dongles | `cm108` | `cm108_gpio = 3` (some use 1 or 4) | | CAT-controlled HF rig | `hamlib` | `hamlib_model`, `device` | | sBitx | `hermes_shm` | — (or `-S`) | | uBitx (HERMES trx_v1, `ubitx_controller`) | `hermes_shm` | — (or `-S`) | The AIOC exposes both a CDC serial port and a CM108-compatible HID endpoint, so either method works. `cm108` needs no device path — Mercury finds it — but the HID endpoint is root-only by default, so it needs a udev rule if Mercury is not running as root. `cm108` works on all three supported platforms, via hidapi: | Platform | hidapi source | Notes | |---|---|---| | Linux | `libhidapi-dev` (`pkg-config`) | Optional — without it Mercury talks to `/dev/hidraw` directly, so a minimal Raspberry Pi build needs no extra package | | macOS | `brew install hidapi` | | | Windows | vendored in `radio_io/hidapi-w64` | Built from source with the rest of the tree, like `hamlib-w64`; no prebuilt library needed | `pkg-config` detection is deliberately skipped for the Windows cross-build: it would find the *host* hidapi and link something that cannot run on the target. ### Restricting network access Mercury's TCP ports listen on every interface, by design: the remote UI, BPQ32 or Pat on another host, and the hosted web app all connect over the network. None of them is authenticated, and the ARQ control port can key the transmitter, so on a network you don't trust, limit who can reach them with a host firewall rather than in Mercury's configuration. The ports, with their defaults: ARQ control 8300 and data 8301 (`-p`, `arq_tcp_base_port`), broadcast 8100 (`-b`) and the UI WebSocket 10000 (`-U`, `ui_port`). This nftables table lets them be reached only from this machine and one LAN; change `192.168.1.0/24` to yours: ``` table inet mercury { chain input { type filter hook input priority filter; policy accept; tcp dport { 8100, 8300, 8301, 10000 } ip saddr { 127.0.0.0/8, 192.168.1.0/24 } accept tcp dport { 8100, 8300, 8301, 10000 } drop } } ``` Its own table and `policy accept` leave every other rule alone. Load it with `sudo nft -f mercury.nft`; to keep it across reboots, add it to `/etc/nftables.conf` and `sudo systemctl enable nftables`. If you change a port, change it here too. ## Documentation **[docs/](docs/README.md)** — the full index, sorted into reference (how Mercury works today), guides (building, signing, Reticulum, sanitizers) and findings (dated records of investigations and why decisions were made). The three you are most likely to want: - [docs/CAROUSEL-ARQ.md](docs/CAROUSEL-ARQ.md) — the ARQ data link: connect, the carousel, the wire formats - [docs/TNC.md](docs/TNC.md) — every TNC command, for driving Mercury from your own software - [docs/MODES.md](docs/MODES.md) — all modes with measured performance Rendered HTML: https://rhizomatica.github.io/mercury/ ## Logging and timing traces - Default run (`./mercury`): logger runs at **INFO** level with timestamps (`[INF]/[WRN]/[ERR]`). - Verbose run (`./mercury -v`): logger runs at **DEBUG** level and includes all detailed ARQ/modem traces (`[DBG]` and `[TMG]`). - Trace run (`./mercury -d`): logger runs at **TRACE** level and additionally logs the raw bytes of every decoded connect frame, so you can see who is calling whom on the channel (`[TRC]`). Implies `-v`. - `./mercury -v -L /tmp/session.log` — write full DEBUG+TIMING log to file. - `./mercury -v -L /tmp/session.log -J` — same, but in **JSONL** format for machine parsing with `jq`. - Text log lines start with the date and time, `2026-11-02 23:15:57.123`, in local time; `[main] log_utc = true` writes them in UTC with a `Z` (`2026-11-02 23:15:57.123Z`), to line them up with BPQ32's or another station's log. - Right after the logger starts, a line names the build: `Mercury 1.9.23 (git 1234abcd)`. - The log file is capped at `[main] log_max_mb` (default 20 MB; 0: no cap). Past it the file moves to `.1`, replacing the one before, and a new file starts, so at most twice the cap is on disk. Each file has a line naming the other. - TX state transitions are logged with timestamps at INFO level as: - `TX enabled (PTT ON)` - `TX disabled (PTT OFF)` - A session's teardown after the host's `DISCONNECT` is logged at INFO level: `DISCONNECT deferred until delivered (up to N s)` or `DISCONNECT: nothing left to deliver, ending now`, then `Teardown starts (caller|callee), N ms after the host's DISCONNECT`, and on the other end `Peer's DISCONNECT received N ms after the host's`. See [docs/CAROUSEL-ARQ.md](docs/CAROUSEL-ARQ.md) for the ARQ data link and [docs/CAROUSEL-SPEC.md](docs/CAROUSEL-SPEC.md) for its specification. ## Reticulum Mercury can carry [Reticulum](https://github.com/markqvist/reticulum) mesh networking over HF via its KISS-over-TCP broadcast port (verified) or as a point-to-point ARQ backbone. See [docs/RETICULUM.md](docs/RETICULUM.md) for the integration architectures and configuration. Mercury can also broadcast a **file** to whoever is listening, with no return path, using a RaptorQ fountain carousel wire-compatible with [hermes-broadcast](https://github.com/Rhizomatica/hermes-broadcast). See [docs/BROADCAST-FILE.md](docs/BROADCAST-FILE.md). ## Physical Layer Mercury builds on the FreeDV / codec2 OFDM data modes developed by David Rowe and contributors, and **extends them with waveforms and link-layer techniques developed by Rhizomatica** for the conditions HERMES actually operates in: long NVIS and regional paths, marginal signal levels, and fading. These modes Mercury uses are ours, not upstream (all modes, with FEC, airtime and measured thresholds: [docs/MODES.md](docs/MODES.md)): | Mode | Bandwidth | Payload | What it is for | |---|---|---|---| | **DATAC15** | 200 Hz | 30 B | Fringe data. Rate-1/3 LDPC, 3 carriers — reaches below the floor of any stock data mode | | **DATAC16** | 200 Hz | 14 B | Control and ACK at the fringe; the mode the whole session depends on | | **DATAC17** | 2250 Hz | 1184 B | Intermediate SNR, roughly 2× the goodput of DATAC1 | | **QAM16C2** | 2250 Hz | 1183 B | Good channels, roughly 2.9× DATAC1 | | **DATAC17W**, **QAM16C2W** | 2750 Hz | 1170 B, 1169 B | BW2750's rungs 5 and 6: DATAC17 and QAM16C2 on 44 carriers | | **DATAN1**, **QAM16N1**, **QAM16N2** | 562 Hz | 243 B, 179 B, 242 B | BW500's rungs 4-6, on 9 carriers | | **MFSK** | 1000 Hz | 98 B | The deepest fringe: non-coherent 32-tone MFSK (50 % frame loss at −11.2 dB on AWGN, DATAC15 −10.3 dB; [measured](docs/MFSK-PORT.md)); the carousel's floor rung, and the carrier of CALLs and tone-pattern ACKs there | | **MFSK500** | 500 Hz | 98 B | The same frame in half the bandwidth (~26.2 s): the floor of a BW500 session, and of a wider one whose ACCEPT went on it (the deep floor) | | **MFSK2K** | 2000 Hz | 98 B | Twice the 1 kHz floor's rate (~6.56 s a frame): rung 1 of BW2300 and BW2750 | Beyond the waveforms, the link layer adds: - **An erasure-coded carousel** ([docs/CAROUSEL-ARQ.md](docs/CAROUSEL-ARQ.md)) — the application's bytes are cut into Reed-Solomon blocks, and the receiver polls for what each block still needs. A lost frame is never resent as such: any other piece of its block replaces it, so a fade costs airtime but not a stall. Rungs move on measured delivery, not on SNR estimates alone. - **Tone-pattern ACKs and NAV headers** at the MFSK floor — 0.64 s patterns detected down to about −14 dB SNR on AWGN, where DATAC16 frames stop near −10 dB, and bound to the session so another pair's patterns are not read as ours. - **Per-mode SNR calibration**, so rung decisions are made on numbers that mean the same thing across modes. - **HARQ with Chase combining** in the decoders — repeats of a failed frame are soft-combined with the original ([measured](docs/HARQ-FINDINGS.md): 0/130 → 61/130 at −5.8 dB at the fading cliff). It is off inside carousel sessions, whose frames are never repeats of each other, and applies to plain (unseeded) frames. Every mode figure above is measured on a calibrated bench (Watterson fading channel, 100-burst trials) that reproduces the published upstream numbers before it is trusted for ours. See [docs/MODES.md](docs/MODES.md) for the full tables, methodology, and the negative results. ## Graphical Interfaces Mercury has three **fully supported** interfaces. All three are maintained by the HERMES team and all three are first-class — pick whichever suits how you operate. **Built-in GUI (Go / Fyne)** — *the simplest way to run Mercury.* The engine and the interface are one binary: no separate modem process to start, no ports to wire up. Waterfall and spectrum, telemetry, radio and audio settings, and a **Mercury Client** chat window for ARQ and broadcast messaging built straight in. With the engine in the same program, the chat window drives it directly, so the TNC ports (8300, 8301, 8100) stay free for uucp, VarAC or another TCP client; one that connects takes the TNC from the window, as it would from another TCP client. The main window's TCP indicator then reads **In app**. Ships as an installer on Windows, a universal `.dmg` on macOS, and `make fyne-ui` on Linux. **Web interface** — runs in a browser, nothing to install, and works against a Mercury running on another machine (a Raspberry Pi at the antenna, say). Included in `docs/app/`, or use it directly at https://rhizomatica.github.io/mercury/app/ **Mercury-qt** — the native Qt desktop client: https://github.com/Rhizomatica/mercury-qt The web and Qt interfaces talk to the engine over its WebSocket interface (`-G`); the built-in GUI links the engine directly, so it needs no flags.
